descriptionChirho: A feeling of joy, satisfaction, or emotional pleasure in something or someone, often used of God's delight in obedience or a person's delight in Torah or wisdom. Appears in theological contexts asking whether God takes delight in sacrifices (1 Sam 15:22, Job 21:21, 22:3), the righteous person whose delight is in YHWH's Torah (Ps 1:2), the delight of God's will prospering (Isa 53:10), and Sabbath delight (Isa 58:3, 13). Also in wisdom literature concerning the delight found in understanding or lack thereof (Eccl 5:4, 12:1, 12:10). Multilingual glosses converge on pleasure vocabulary: مَسَرَّة (Arb, joy/delight), Wohlgefallen/Gefallen (Deu, pleasure/delight), plaisir/delice (Fra), आनंद/प्रसन्नता/खुशि (Hin, joy/happiness), 기쁨/기뻐 (Kor, joy), deleite/agrado (Spa, delight/pleasure).

A want, longing, intention, or expressed will, including the sovereign purpose or plan of God and human desires or wishes. Distinguished from the 'delight' sense by its volitional and purposive orientation rather than emotional satisfaction. Appears prominently in contexts of royal and divine will: Solomon's desire for building projects (1 Kgs 5:8-10, 9:11, 10:13), God's purpose that will be accomplished (Isa 44:28, 46:10, 48:14), and personal desire or pleasure-seeking (Isa 58:13, your pleasures; 2 Sam 23:5; Ps 107:30). Multilingual glosses shift toward volitional vocabulary: رَغْبَة (Arb, desire/wish), desire (Eng), désir (Fra), इच्छा (Hin, wish/desire), 소원/원하는 것 (Kor, wish/desired thing), deseo/voluntad (Spa, desire/will).

A thing, business matter, or concern under consideration, used in a neutral, non-emotional sense to refer to activities, occupations, or the general course of events. This sense is characteristic of Ecclesiastes, where חֵפֶץ refers to the appointed activities or purposes that govern human life: 'For every matter there is a time and a way' (Eccl 3:1, 3:17, 8:6). Also 'the end of the matter' (Eccl 5:8). The English gloss 'matter' and Korean 일 (il, 'affair/matter') clearly distinguish this from the emotional 'delight' or volitional 'desire' senses. Hindi इच्छा and Spanish propósito/asunto also reflect this pragmatic, non-emotional usage in context.

A valuable, precious, or coveted object understood in a concrete, material sense rather than as an abstract feeling or volition. This sense appears in wisdom literature where precious stones or jewels are compared to wisdom: 'All your desires cannot compare with her' (Prov 3:15, 8:11), where the plural חֲפָצִים refers to desirable possessions or treasures. Also in Isaiah 54:12, where gates are made of 'stones of delight' (precious gems). The Arabic أَشْيَاء (things/objects), Spanish cosas preciosas (precious things), Hindi इच्छाएँ (desires, used concretely), and Korean 소원들 (wishes/desires) all support the concrete-material nuance of desirable objects rather than abstract pleasure.
